lab_title: Demystifying Retrograde Motion: Heliocentric vs. Geocentric Perspectives
top_level_objectives: Identify and describe the visual phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion from the perspective of an Earth observer.
Compare and contrast the geocentric (epicycle-based) and heliocentric explanations for retrograde motion.
Explain how the relative orbital speeds of Earth and outer planets produce apparent retrograde loops during planetary oppositions.
Analyze how a planet's distance from the Sun influences the frequency and apparent size of its retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the mystery of retrograde motion by allowing students to observe Mars's erratic path through the night sky from a ground-based perspective over several months.
key_visuals: A 3D semi-dome representing the night sky over a desert landscape, populated with major constellations.
A glowing red marker for Mars that moves night-by-night, leaving a persistent, luminous path tracer in the sky.
A time-elapsed calendar UI showing the progression of days and months.
student_actions: Drag a timeline slider to fast-forward time over several months and watch Mars drift eastward, slow down, loop westward (retrograde), and resume eastward motion.
Tap on specific dates on the path tracer to log when the direction of motion changes.
Select the 'Show Constellations' toggle to identify which background star groups Mars passes through during its loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the historical geocentric model to understand how ancient astronomers used complex geometric constructs (epicycles and deferents) to explain the apparent retrograde loops.
key_visuals: An interactive 3D geocentric model with a static Earth at the center.
Mars orbiting on a small circle (the epicycle), which itself orbits along a larger circular path (the deferent) around Earth.
A dynamic projection line showing Mars's apparent line-of-sight path as seen from Earth onto a distant celestial sphere.
student_actions: Rotate the geocentric model to view it from different angles, experiencing the 3D geometry.
Adjust sliders to change the speed of the epicycle and the deferent, observing how it alters the shape and frequency of the resulting loops.
Tap highlighted nodes to reveal historical text boxes explaining why Ptolemy introduced this mechanism.

scenes.brief_purpose: Shift to a top-down, out-of-solar-system perspective to view Earth and Mars orbiting the Sun at their natural, differing speeds.
key_visuals: A top-down solar system model featuring a central glowing Sun, Earth, and Mars on their respective coplanar, concentric orbits.
Orbital velocity vectors showing that Earth moves faster on its inner orbit than Mars does on its outer orbit.
A dynamic, color-coded line of sight connecting Earth and Mars, pointing toward a distant background star field.
student_actions: Play, pause, and step through the orbital simulation to observe Earth 'catching up' to and passing Mars.
Rotate the orbital plane in AR space to view the system from both overhead and edge-on perspectives.
Toggle a 'Line of Sight' visual aid to see how the projected direction of Mars against the background stars changes as Earth passes it.

scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce the physics of relative motion using a familiar real-world analogy: passing a slower car on a highway.
key_visuals: A straight, two-lane highway segment in AR with a distant mountain range on the horizon acting as background stars.
A fast blue car (representing Earth) in the left lane and a slower red car (representing Mars) in the right lane.
An overlay camera showing the view looking out the passenger window of the blue car toward the red car.
student_actions: Press an 'Accelerate' button to initiate the passing maneuver.
Observe the passenger-window feed to see the red car appear to drift backward against the distant mountains during the pass, despite both cars moving forward.
Tap on-screen markers to correlate 'approaching', 'passing', and 'leaving behind' with the stages of retrograde motion.

scenes.brief_purpose: Directly link the top-down heliocentric motion of Earth and Mars with the corresponding apparent sky path observed from Earth's surface.
key_visuals: A synchronized, split-view AR model: one side shows the top-down orbital motion, and the other shows the Earth's night sky dome.
Numbered markers (1 through 5) placed at key orbital positions along the paths of Earth and Mars, with matching numbered markers on the sky dome's path tracer.
A sweeping sightline that connects the two views in real-time.
student_actions: Manually scrub the synchronized time controller frame-by-frame through the five key orbital stages.
Match orbital configurations (e.g., Opposition, where Sun, Earth, and Mars align) with the peak of the retrograde loop on the sky dome.
Place interactive labels on the orbital model identifying the zones of 'Direct Motion', 'Stationary Points', and 'Retrograde Motion'.

scenes.brief_purpose: Compare Mars's retrograde behavior with that of Jupiter and Saturn to understand how distance from Earth and the Sun affects the phenomenon.
key_visuals: An expanded heliocentric model showing Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in their respective orbits.
A side-by-side celestial projection panel showing the night-sky paths of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn over a matching timescale.
Data readouts displaying orbital period, distance from the Sun, and loop duration for each planet.
student_actions: Select Jupiter or Saturn to activate their orbits and observe their relative orbital speeds compared to Earth.
Analyze the size and frequency of the loops for each planet on the celestial projection panel.
Complete an interactive sorting puzzle, ranking the three planets based on the size of their apparent retrograde loops and explaining how distance diminishes the relative-motion effect.
